# MOSAICS

**MOSAICS** (*Massive-scale Observational Survey Acquisition and Cross-correlation System*) assembles machine-learning datasets out of astronomical archives. Given sky positions or survey selection rules, MOSAICS queries remote and local catalogues, crossmatches multi-wavelength photometry and spectroscopy, fetches calibrated image cutouts and 1D spectra, and writes the combined tables, fixed-shape image tensors, and variable-length spectral arrays into Apache Arrow / Lance datasets accompanied by reproducible `scireport` quality reports.

## The three data products

::::{grid} 1 1 3 3
:gutter: 3

:::{grid-item-card}
**[1. Multi-survey catalogues](concepts/targets-pipeline.md)**

Extract and crossmatch optical, UV, and infrared photometry (`ls11`, `gaia3`, `galex`, `hsc3`, `vhs5`, `wise`, `euclidq1`, ...) with spectroscopic redshifts (`desi1`, `sdss17`, `lamost11`, `6dfgs`, `2dfgrs`, `hasp`, ...) or Rubin/LSST Data Previews (`lsstdp1`, `lsstdp2`), homogenised to AB magnitudes and microjansky ($\mu\text{Jy}$) fluxes.
:::

:::{grid-item-card}
**[2. Calibrated image cutouts](concepts/cutout-backends.md)**

Retrieve multi-band FITS/JPEG image stamps across 17 imaging surveys via five interchangeable backends (`hips`, `hips --local`, `lsv`, `nersc`, `sia`, `vsa`) and store them as fixed-shape 3D tensors in a resumable Lance dataset.
:::

:::{grid-item-card}
**[3. Variable-length 1D spectra](concepts/spectra.md)**

Download 1D spectra across 7 spectroscopic surveys via four backends (`url`, `template`, `sparcl`, `desi-healpix`) into parallel `large_list<float32>` (`flux`, `error`, `wavelength`) and `large_list<bool>` (`mask`) Arrow columns.
:::
::::

## How the pieces fit

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  LIB["Survey library<br/>defs/surveys/*.yaml"] --> Q["mosaics-query<br/>archive queries"]
  LIB --> X["mosaics-crossmatch<br/>any table against any surveys"]
  LIB --> T["mosaics-targets<br/>multi-survey catalogue"]
  LIB --> C["mosaics-cutout<br/>image stamps"]
  LIB --> S["mosaics-spectrum<br/>1D spectra"]
  X --> XT[("Matched table")]
  X -- "--fov" --> FOV["mosaics-fov<br/>cutout size"]
  T --> TC[("Targets catalogue<br/>with fov")]
  FOV --> XT
  TC --> C
  TC --> S
  C --> CD[("Cutout dataset<br/>Lance")]
  S --> SD[("Spectrum dataset<br/>Lance")]
```

## Three-command tour

Run all commands from a repository checkout after `uv sync`:

```console
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.query cone --service vizier --table "VII/250/2dfgrs" --columns SEQNUM RAJ2000 DEJ2000 z --ra 180.0 --dec 0.0 --radius 0.5 -o 2df_cone.parquet
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.cutout full -t test/objects_sample_1k.csv -o cutouts.lance --config defs/cutout.yaml --size 64 --fov-unit arcmin
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.spectrum sdss17 -t test/objects_sample_1k.csv -o sdss17_spectra.lance --snr-floor 2.0
```

# Installation & Credentials

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Access to the private `nmcardoso/mosaics` GitHub repository is required to clone and install MOSAICS. Always run MOSAICS from a repository checkout so that the survey definitions in `defs/` and SQL queries in `defs/surveys/*.sql` resolve relative to the checkout root.

## 1. Clone and install with `uv`

MOSAICS requires Python $\ge 3.12$ and is managed with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/):

```bash
git clone git@github.com:nmcardoso/mosaics.git
cd mosaics
uv sync
```

`uv sync` installs `mosaics` in editable mode inside `.venv` along with all runtime dependencies (`pyarrow`, `pylance`, `duckdb`, `lsdb`, `astropy`, `reproject`, `scireport[astro,pdf]`, etc.) and registers nine console scripts (`mosaics-cutout`, `mosaics-query`, `mosaics-spectrum`, `mosaics-targets`, `mosaics-crossmatch`, `mosaics-fov`, `mosaics-hipscat`, `mosaics-proxy`, `mosaics-report`).

Confirm the installation:

```console
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.cutout --help
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.targets --help
```

## 2. System packages for PDF reports

Every pipeline report (`mosaics-targets`, `mosaics-crossmatch`, `mosaics-report`) always writes a sealed `.scireport.zip` bundle and chapter-split Markdown files (`report/md/*.md`). Rendering the print-ready PDF (`report/pdf/report.pdf`) uses WeasyPrint, which requires the system Pango and HarfBuzz shared libraries:

```bash
# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y libpango-1.0-0 libpangoft2-1.0-0 libharfbuzz-subset0
```

If Pango is unavailable on a headless cluster node, pass `--no-report-pdf` (or `--no-pdf` on `mosaics-report`) to produce the `.scireport.zip` bundle and Markdown chapters without invoking WeasyPrint.

## 3. Archive credentials

Most astronomical archives queried by MOSAICS (CDS VizieR, CDS HiPS/hips2fits, NERSC Legacy Survey sweeps and bricks, STScI MAST, LAMOST, WFAU SIA/VSA, LINCC/CDS HATS servers, SDSS SAS) answer anonymously. Three services support or require account credentials, read from environment variables or a `.env` file in the checkout root:

| Archive / Provider | Environment variables | When needed |
|---|---|---|
| **Rubin Science Platform (`lsst`)** | `LSST_TOKEN` (or `LSST_PASSWORD` / `LSST_PASS`), overridable via `--lsst-token` | Required for the Rubin surveys (`lsstdp1`, `lsstdp2`) in every `mosaics-crossmatch` command (`run`, `moc`, `jobs`, `kill`, `del`). Never read from a YAML file. |
| **NSF NOIRLab Astro Data Lab (`adl`)** | `DATALAB_USERNAME`, `DATALAB_PASSWORD` (overridable via `--username` / `--password`) | Optional for public tables (`gaia_dr3.gaia_source`, `allwise.source`, `ukidss_dr11plus.lassource`); required for proprietary access or extended MyDB storage. |
| **SciServer CasJobs (`sciserver`)** | `SCISERVER_USERNAME`, `SCISERVER_PASSWORD` (overridable via `--username` / `--password`) | Required when querying SciServer CasJobs (`--provider sciserver`) or cleaning up MyDB tables (`mosaics-query sweep`). |
| **Weights & Biases (`--wandb`)** | `WANDB_API_KEY` | Optional; used only when `--wandb` telemetry is enabled on `cutout`, `spectrum`, or `targets`. |

## 4. Download cache directories

Field-based cutout backends (`hips --local`, `nersc`, `sia`, `vsa`) and the `nersc` catalogue provider cache downloaded tiles, bricks, and sweep slices on disk under `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/mosaics` (default `~/.cache/mosaics`), capped by `--cache-size-gb` (default `50.0` GB LRU). You can point individual caches at fast scratch storage with environment variables:

| Environment variable | Default path | What it stores |
|---|---|---|
| `MOSAICS_HIPS_CACHE` | `~/.cache/mosaics/hips` | Downloaded HiPS tiles for `hips --local`. |
| `MOSAICS_BRICK_CACHE` | `~/.cache/mosaics/bricks` | Legacy Survey coadd bricks from NERSC (`cutout nersc`). |
| `MOSAICS_FIELD_CACHE` | `~/.cache/mosaics/fields` | SIA and VSA survey frames before local WCS reprojection. |
| `MOSAICS_TRACTOR_CACHE` | `~/.cache/mosaics/tractor` | Pruned NERSC sweep and tractor Parquet slices (`catalog` / `targets`). |


# Quickstart

This walk-through runs the three core workflows—image cutouts, 1D spectra, and catalogue queries—using the sample target lists shipped in `test/`.

## 1. Preview and fetch multi-survey image cutouts

Given a table with target positions (`id`, `ra`, `dec`), `mosaics-cutout full` routes your requested surveys and passbands across the enabled cutout backends defined in `defs/full.yaml`.

First, inspect the routing plan without making any network requests (`--plan`):

```console
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.cutout full -t test/objects_sample_1k.csv -o cutouts.lance --config defs/cutout.yaml --size 96 --fov-unit arcmin --plan
```

Run the extraction (writing batches to `cutouts.lance` as they complete so an interrupted run can be resumed with `--resume`):

```console
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.cutout full -t test/objects_sample_1k.csv -o cutouts.lance --config defs/cutout.yaml --size 96 --fov-unit arcmin --batch-size 128
```

## 2. Fetch 1D spectra for a target table

Each spectroscopic survey in `defs/surveys/` has its own subcommand under `mosaics-spectrum` (plus `full` to run multiple spectroscopic surveys into one Lance dataset).

For example, to fetch SDSS DR17 coadded spectra for a table carrying `sdss17_plate`, `sdss17_mjd`, `sdss17_fiberid` (or to run all configured spectroscopic adapters with `full`):

```console
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.spectrum sdss17 -t test/objects_sample_1k.csv -o sdss17_spectra.lance --snr-floor 2.0
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.spectrum full -t test/objects_sample_1k.csv -o all_spectra.lance --config defs/full.yaml --snr-floor 2.0
```

## 3. Query a remote astronomical catalogue

Use `mosaics-query` to run a cone search, a sky box (`region`), or a custom ADQL/SQL query against any supported provider (`tap`, `adl`, `sciserver`, `crossid`, `local`, `nersc`):

```console
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.query cone --provider tap --service vizier --table "VII/259/6dfgs" --columns 6dFGS RAJ2000 DEJ2000 cz --ra 180.0 --dec -10.0 --radius 1.0 -o 6dfgs_cone.parquet
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.query region --provider adl --table gaia_dr3.gaia_source --ra-range 180.0 180.2 --dec-range 0.0 0.2 --columns source_id ra dec phot_g_mean_mag -o gaia_box.parquet
```

## 4. Match a table against surveys, and size its cutouts

`mosaics-crossmatch run` joins the columns of one or more surveys onto a table of positions; with `--fov` it also adds the size of the cutout that frames each galaxy of one of them. The shipped `wise` file needs no login:

```console
$ uv run -m mosaics.crossmatch.cli run --survey surveys/wise -i test/objects_sample_1k.csv -o matched.parquet --dry-run
$ uv run -m mosaics.crossmatch.cli run --survey extensions/ls11-datalab -i test/objects_sample_1k.csv -o galaxies.parquet --fov ls11
```

The first prints what it would send and sends nothing. See [crossmatching](../concepts/crossmatch.md) and [field of view](../concepts/field-of-view.md).

## 5. Build a multi-survey target catalogue

`mosaics-targets` runs the eight-stage target selection and multi-survey crossmatch pipeline over declination strips (`--dec-range`), writing sky-cell stores that resume automatically and producing a homogenised Parquet/Lance catalogue alongside a `scireport` bundle and PDF report:

```console
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.targets --config defs/targets.yaml -o ./targets_run --dec-range 0.0 1.0 --plan plan.yaml
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.targets --config defs/targets.yaml -o ./targets_run --dec-range 0.0 1.0
```


# End-to-End Recipes

Each recipe below is self-contained: it shows the input file or YAML configuration, the exact CLI command, and the resulting output files and columns.

---

## Recipe 1: Extract calibrated optical + NIR cutouts from a custom survey subset

**Goal:** Given a CSV of galaxy coordinates (`id,ra,dec`), extract $128 \times 128$ pixel cutouts in Legacy Survey DR11 ($g, r, z$ via NERSC bricks) and SkyMapper DR4 ($g, r, i$ via local HiPS tile rendering) into a single Lance dataset.

**1. Input table (`targets.csv`):**

```text
id,ra,dec
1001,180.1234,-5.4321
1002,180.2345,-5.3210
```

**2. Entrypoint configuration (`my_cutouts.yaml`):**

```yaml
surveys:
  - surveys/ls11
  - surveys/skymapper4

overrides:
  surveys/ls11:
    cutout:
      - adapter: nersc
        adapter_params:
          bands: grz
          data_release: dr11
        bands: [g, r, z]
```

Relative paths in `surveys:` resolve against the file's directory, then `$CWD`, then `defs/`. `surveys:` lists the survey files the run covers and `overrides:` changes the ones its key names.

**3. Command:**

```console
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.cutout full -t test/objects_sample_1k.csv -o cutouts_opt.lance --config defs/cutout.yaml --size 128 --fov-unit arcmin
```

**4. Output:**
- `cutouts_opt.lance/`: Lance dataset containing `id`, `ra`, `dec`, and fixed-shape `float32` tensor columns `cutout_ls11_g`, `cutout_ls11_r`, `cutout_ls11_z`, `cutout_skymapper4_g`, `cutout_skymapper4_r`, `cutout_skymapper4_i` of shape `(1, 128, 128)`, with per-column calibration stored in the Arrow field metadata (`mosaics_unit`, `mosaics_scale`, `mosaics_offset`).
- `cutouts_opt.failures.parquet`: sidecar listing any target/service pair that failed, ready for `--retry-failed`.

---

## Recipe 2: Resume an interrupted cutout or spectrum run and retry transient archive errors

**Goal:** Continue a long extraction after a network interruption or `Ctrl-C`, then re-attempt only the rows that failed during the initial pass.

**Commands:**

```console
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.cutout full -t test/objects_sample_1k.csv -o cutouts_opt.lance --config defs/cutout.yaml --resume
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.cutout full -t test/objects_sample_1k.csv -o cutouts_opt.lance --config defs/cutout.yaml --resume --retry-failed --fill-missing rewrite
```

- `--resume` reads the existing key column (`id`) from `cutouts_opt.lance` and skips every row already committed.
- `--retry-failed` reads `cutouts_opt.failures.parquet`, re-fetches only the failed `(id, service)` pairs, and with `--fill-missing rewrite` patches the recovered tensors back into `cutouts_opt.lance` in place.

---

## Recipe 3: Crossmatch a local table against Rubin/LSST Data Preview 2 (`dp2.Object`)

**Goal:** Match a local Parquet catalogue against `dp2.Object` on the Rubin Science Platform, filtering out positions outside the release footprint beforehand so only in-footprint targets cross the wire.

**Commands:**

```console
$ uv run -m mosaics.crossmatch.cli moc --survey surveys/lsstdp2 -o lsst-dp2-moc.fits
$ uv run -m mosaics.crossmatch.cli run --survey surveys/lsstdp2 -i test/objects_sample_1k.csv -o matched_lsst.parquet --filter-moc
```

The radius, the columns and the release come from the shipped `lsstdp2` survey file. Name the footprint under `overrides:` in a job file (`crossmatch: {moc: lsst-dp2-moc.fits}`) so `--filter-moc` finds it, or describe the source on the command line with no survey file at all:

```console
$ uv run -m mosaics.crossmatch.cli run -i test/objects_sample_1k.csv -o matched_lsst.parquet --adapter lsst --param release=dp2 --table dp2.Object --radius "1 arcsec" --columns objectId coord_ra coord_dec "[ugrizy]_cModelMag" --moc lsst-dp2-moc.fits --filter-moc
```

**Output:**
- `lsst-dp2-moc.fits`: Multi-Order Coverage map built once from `dp2.CoaddPatches`.
- `matched_lsst.parquet`: All input columns preserved plus the matched `dp2.Object` columns, the separation and the number of counterparts.
- `matched_lsst.crossmatch.yaml` and `matched_lsst.report/`: Machine-readable run account, sealed `crossmatch.scireport.zip` bundle, chapter Markdown files in `md/`, and `pdf/report.pdf`.

**Several surveys at once.** A job file lists them and may change any survey inline; every key is an option of `run`:

```yaml
# runs/two-surveys.yaml
surveys: [surveys/wise, surveys/gaia3]
input: test/objects_sample_1k.csv
output: matched.parquet
overrides:
  surveys/wise:
    crossmatch:
      radius: 2 arcsec
```

```console
$ uv run -m mosaics.crossmatch.cli run -c runs/two-surveys.yaml
```

**Extending a shipped survey.** The shipped survey files are a library you extend rather than edit. To match `wise` at 2 arcseconds against your own copy of the table, write a survey file that extends the shipped one and name it:

```yaml
# my_wise.yaml
extends: surveys/wise.yaml
crossmatch:
  radius: 2 arcsec
catalog:
  - name: wise
    type: photometric
    adapter: tap
    adapter_params:
      service: https://example.org/tap
      table: my.allwise_copy
```

```console
$ uv run -m mosaics.crossmatch.cli run --survey my_wise -i test/objects_sample_1k.csv -o matched_wise.parquet
```

The slug stays `wise`, so the columns keep their `wise_` prefix. The file is found next to where you run the command, and `extends:` finds `surveys/wise.yaml` in the package's `defs/`.

**Adding the cutout size.** `--fov SURVEY` adds the `fov` column from the shape and magnitude columns that survey brought, and `--hle` sizes it with the half-light ellipse alone (see [Field of view](../concepts/field-of-view.md)). `mosaics-cutout` then needs `--fov-unit arcsec`:

```console
$ uv run -m mosaics.crossmatch.cli run --survey extensions/ls11-datalab -i test/objects_sample_1k.csv -o matched_ls11.parquet --fov ls11 --hle
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.cutout lsv -t matched_ls11.parquet -o lsv_grz.lance --layer ls-dr11 --bands grz --size 96 --fov-unit arcsec
```

---

## Recipe 4: Run a multi-node extraction across SSH worker machines

**Goal:** Spread archive requests across multiple machines (`node1.example.org`, `node2.example.org`) to multiply per-IP archive rate limits while keeping all orchestration and storage on the main node.

**Commands:**

```console
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.proxy keygen
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.proxy server --proxy-port 8888 --tunnel-port 8022 --stats-port 8889
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.targets --config defs/targets.yaml -o ./targets_run --dec-range -5.0 5.0 --proxy http://127.0.0.1:8888
```

**Output:**
- The proxy server deploys and heartbeats lightweight worker processes over SSH, load-balancing per-origin requests by live worker goodput and latency.
- When `mosaics-targets` finishes, it queries the proxy stats endpoint, merges per-node throughput and traffic into `targets_report.yaml`, and renders the multi-node execution chapter in the report.


# Run a worker

This page is for collaborators who lend a machine to a MOSAICS download. A *worker* is a small program that makes archive requests on behalf of the main node, so the download is spread over more than one IP address and stays inside each archive's per-IP rate limit (see [Archive rate limits](../concepts/archives.md)). You receive one command from the person who runs the main node; this page says what it does, what it sends and how to stop and remove it.

## What the command does

The command you received has the form below, where `NAME` is the name you choose for your worker (1 to 64 letters, digits or hyphens):

```console
$ curl -sL <the address you were given> | sh -s -- NAME
```

It needs no root rights and installs nothing outside two folders in your home directory. In order:

1. A short shell script checks the name and that the machine is Linux on x86_64, downloads a small launcher program (a static binary of about 2 MB) and checks its SHA-256 against the value written in the script. A launcher that does not match is not run.
2. The launcher finds `uv` on your `PATH`, or downloads a pinned release of it into `~/.mosaics/bin` after checking its SHA-256. It never pipes a downloaded installer into a shell.
3. The launcher downloads the worker's encrypted payload, checks its SHA-256, decrypts it into a private temporary folder (mode 0700) and starts the worker with `uv`, which fetches Python 3.12 if the machine has none and the worker's few dependencies from PyPI.
4. The worker makes its own SSH host key on the first run, reads the announcement of where the main node is, logs in to the institute's SSH host and tells the main node its name and its [machine data](#what-is-sent-and-where-it-is-kept). From then on it answers heartbeats and carries the requests the main node sends it. The worker logs each step as it goes, including the SSH host and port it connects to.
5. When the worker ends, the launcher deletes the temporary folder.

A second run with the same name finds everything cached and starts in a few seconds. A new release of the worker is picked up when you run the command again.

## Requirements

- Linux on x86_64 (the script refuses anything else).
- `curl` or `wget`, and `sha256sum` or `shasum`.
- Outbound HTTPS, to download the launcher, the payload and (if needed) `uv`, Python and the worker's dependencies, and to look up your public address.
- Outbound SSH, to the institute's login host. The login host uses a non-standard port, which the worker prints when it starts, so a firewall that only allows port 22 out will block it.
- Nothing inbound: the worker dials out and opens no port on your machine.

## What is sent, and where it is kept

When it registers, the worker sends the main node the data below. Each item is best effort and is left empty when it cannot be read.

| Item | What is sent |
|---|---|
| Name and user | The name you chose, your short and fully qualified host name, and the login name of the user running the worker. |
| System | Operating system, kernel release, distribution name, CPU architecture. |
| Hardware | Number of logical CPUs, CPU model, installed memory in GB. |
| Process | Python version, worker release and build, protocol version, process id, start time (UTC), local time zone. |
| Addresses | The addresses of your network interfaces and of your default route (these can be private addresses), and your **public IP address**. The worker looks the public address up with one request to a public service (`api.ipify.org`, else `1.1.1.1`) when it starts. |
| Machine id | The first 16 hexadecimal characters of a SHA-256 hash of the machine id, never the id itself. It lets the main node tell machines apart. |
| Environment | Whether the worker runs inside a container or WSL. |

Nothing else is read: no file contents, no environment variables, no browsing data and no list of your processes.

The main node keeps this data in two places, both private to the people who run it. A **ledger** file on the main node records one entry when you connect and one when you leave, with the data above and what the session carried (requests, bytes and the archives they went to). If the operator reports to Weights & Biases, a private project holds the same entries. The ledger and the report are used to credit each worker for what it carried and to tell machines apart. They are not published. If you want your data removed, ask the operator.

The requests themselves pass through your machine. Your public IP address appears in the logs of the archives that serve them, and your connection carries the downloaded bytes. HTTPS traffic stays encrypted between the main node's pipeline and the archive; the worker only opens the connection. Ask the operator how much data to expect, since it depends on the run, and run the worker on a connection where that is acceptable.

## What the main node can ask of your machine

The main node can ask the worker only to open TCP connections to a host and port, and to answer heartbeats. It cannot start a program, read a file or open a shell on your machine. By default the worker accepts destination ports 80 and 443 and refuses every destination that is not on the public internet: loopback, private (for example 10.x, 172.16 to 172.31 and 192.168.x), link-local, shared (carrier-grade NAT) and IPv6 unique-local addresses. A host name is looked up on your machine and refused when any of its addresses is one of those, so a web service on your own network, for example a router or a department server, cannot be reached through the worker. Inside the public internet the worker still opens a connection to any host on those ports. If you want to limit it to the archives it should reach, add options after the name; they are passed through:

```console
$ curl -sL <the address you were given> | sh -s -- NAME --allow-origin '*.cds.unistra.fr' --allow-origin 'irsa.ipac.caltech.edu' --allow-port 443
```

`--allow-origin` takes a hostname pattern and can be repeated; `--allow-port` can be repeated too. A request outside the list is refused and the refusal appears in the worker's log. `--allow-private` lifts the refusal of non-public addresses; use it only for an archive mirror on a private network.

The worker logs in to the institute's SSH host with a login that belongs to the pool and is part of the release. It is used for forwarding the tunnel and is not a login to your machine. Whether several machines may share that login is a question for the institute that hosts it; the operator checks it.

## Stop it

- **Ctrl-C** in the terminal closes the tunnel at once. A request that had not yet received its first byte is placed on another worker by the main node; a download in progress is retried by the pipeline.
- **`SIGTERM`** to the launcher (for example `kill -TERM <pid>`, or `kill -TERM -<pgid>` for the whole process group) **drains** the worker: it stops accepting new requests, waits for the live ones to finish (up to 300 seconds), then leaves. A second `SIGTERM` closes it at once.
- A worker that was told by the main node to drain also leaves on its own.

The main node notices a dead worker within a few heartbeats (about 30 seconds) and stops sending it requests.

## Where files go, and how to remove them

| Where | What |
|---|---|
| `~/.cache/mosaics-worker/bin/` | The launcher, named by its SHA-256. |
| `~/.cache/mosaics-worker/` | The encrypted payload, named by its SHA-256. |
| `~/.mosaics/proxy/` | The worker's SSH host key, `NAME_worker_host_key` and its public half. A worker that restarts under the same name keeps its identity. |
| `~/.mosaics/bin/` | `uv`, only if the machine had none. |
| `$TMPDIR/mosaics-worker-*` | The decrypted payload while the worker runs. Deleted at exit; a folder left by a crash is removed by the next launch once it is an hour old. |
| `uv`'s own folders | The Python 3.12 that `uv` installs when the machine has none. This is `uv`'s normal location and you may keep it. |

To remove everything the worker made:

```console
$ rm -rf ~/.cache/mosaics-worker ~/.mosaics/proxy ~/.mosaics/bin
```

If you also use MOSAICS on the machine, keep the rest of `~/.mosaics`.

## Keep it running

A worker ends when its terminal closes. Two ways to keep it running:

**`tmux` (or `screen`).** The simplest. Start the worker inside a session, detach with `Ctrl-b d`, and come back with `tmux attach`:

```console
$ tmux new -s worker
$ curl -sL <the address you were given> | sh -s -- NAME
```

**systemd, as a user service.** Save the script once, and let the service fetch it fresh at every start, because a saved script names one release of the launcher and the site keeps only the current and the previous release. Create `~/.config/systemd/user/mosaics-worker.service` with the lines below, replacing `NAME` and the address:

```ini
[Unit]
Description=MOSAICS proxy worker

[Service]
ExecStartPre=/bin/sh -c 'curl -fsSL "<the address you were given>" -o "%h/.cache/mosaics-worker.sh"'
ExecStart=/bin/sh %h/.cache/mosaics-worker.sh NAME
KillMode=mixed
TimeoutStopSec=330
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=60

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target
```

Then run `systemctl --user daemon-reload`, `systemctl --user enable --now mosaics-worker` and, so that it survives your logout, `loginctl enable-linger $USER`.

`KillMode=mixed` matters. The launcher puts the worker in its own process group and relays the signals it gets. systemd's default, `control-group`, sends `SIGTERM` to every process of the service at once, so the worker would receive it twice, once directly and once from the launcher, and the second `SIGTERM` closes it without draining. With `KillMode=mixed`, systemd signals only the launcher, which drains the worker; whatever is left after `TimeoutStopSec` (longer than the 300-second drain) is killed. `systemctl --user stop mosaics-worker` therefore drains.

## For the operator: see who is connected

The main node serves a live list of its workers only when it is started with `--stats-port PORT`; the endpoint is off by default and bound to the proxy's own address. `GET /stats` then shows each worker's name, host name, public address, current requests and totals per archive, and `POST /drain?worker=ID` drains one. After the fact, `mosaics-proxy workers` prints the contribution of each name from the ledger. The commands and options are in the [`mosaics-proxy` reference](../cli/proxy.md).


# Long Runs, Resume & Failure Sidecars

Astronomical extractions routinely span hundreds of thousands to tens of millions of targets and run for hours or days. MOSAICS is designed around the assumption that **runs will be interrupted** and **individual targets will fail**.

## 1. Batched commits and `--resume`

Every cutout and spectrum extraction divides the target table into batches (`--batch-size`, default `256` for cutouts and `512` for spectra). As soon as a batch finishes downloading and decoding, it is appended to the output Lance dataset on disk before the next batch begins.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  T["Target table"] --> K{"Unique key column?"}
  K -- no --> X["Rejected before any request"]
  K -- yes --> R{"--resume and the<br/>dataset exists?"}
  R -- yes --> S["Skip the committed keys"] --> B
  R -- no --> B["Next batch"]
  B --> F["Download and decode"]
  F -- ok --> A["Append the batch to the Lance dataset"]
  F -- "a target fails" --> N["Row written with a null cell;<br/>record in .failures.parquet"] --> A
  A --> B
  A --> RF["Later: --retry-failed repeats only<br/>the (target, service) pairs in the sidecar"]
```

- **Unique key requirement:** Every run requires a unique target identifier column (`--id-col`, defaulting to `id`, or a generated `mosaics_id` column when `--id-col` is omitted and no `id` column is present). Duplicate keys in the input table are rejected immediately before any requests are sent, because `--resume` relies on the key column to determine which targets are already stored.
- **Resuming (`--resume`):** Passing `--resume` inspects the existing Lance dataset, reads the committed key values, and skips those rows so work continues from the first uncommitted batch.

```console
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.cutout hips -t test/objects_sample_1k.csv -o cutouts.lance --hips-id CDS/P/PanSTARRS/DR1/g --resume
```

## 2. In-band failures and the `.failures.parquet` sidecar

A failed request or corrupt archive file never aborts a batch or a run. Instead:

1. The row is still written to the Lance dataset in its batch, with an Arrow `null` in the affected image or spectrum column(s).
2. A structured failure record is appended to `<output>.failures.parquet` beside the Lance dataset, recording the target key, the service label (`<survey>:<adapter>:<band>`), the HTTP status or error category, and the failure message.

## 3. Retrying failed targets (`--retry-failed`)

Once a run finishes, you can re-attempt only the failed `(target, service)` pairs recorded in `<output>.failures.parquet`:

```console
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.cutout full -t test/objects_sample_1k.csv -o cutouts.lance --retry-failed --fill-missing rewrite
```

- For **cutouts**, `--fill-missing` controls how recovered stamps are written: `null` (re-fetch only rows where the image is null) or `rewrite` (patch individual band columns in place inside the existing Lance dataset).
- For **spectra**, `--fill-missing rewrite` is refused by design: a spectrum's columns (`flux`, `error`, `wavelength`, `mask`) are parallel variable-length arrays of a single observation and must succeed or fail as an atomic group.

## 4. Cooperative interruption (`Ctrl-C`)

Pressing `Ctrl-C` (`SIGINT`) triggers a cooperative stop across all worker threads and asynchronous downloads:

- Queued tasks are cancelled immediately without starting new HTTP requests.
- Active retry backoff sleeps and streaming file downloads terminate early.
- Interrupted tasks are **never** recorded as failed in `.failures.parquet` or sky-cell ledgers—only completed batches or settled sky cells are kept on disk, leaving the dataset clean for `--resume`.


# Archive Rate Limits, Mirrors & Multi-Node Execution

Astronomical archives enforce strict per-IP concurrency limits and request-rate ceilings. MOSAICS manages archive traffic through four mechanisms: per-origin request caps, windowed rate limiters, dynamic mirror pools, and optional multi-node execution across SSH workers.

## 1. Per-origin concurrency caps and retries

Every HTTP transport in MOSAICS enforces a per-origin concurrency limit (`--max-per-origin`, default `4` concurrent requests per `scheme://host:port`) alongside global concurrency (`--concurrency` / `--workers`).

- Transient HTTP failures (`408`, `429`, `500`, `502`, `503`, `504`, timeouts, and connection resets) are retried with exponential backoff (`--retries`, default `5`, and `--timeout`).
- Every failed HTTP exchange—even one that a subsequent retry recovers—is logged at `ERR` level and counted in the per-service request ledger so archive instability is visible in logs and run reports.
- Services that publish explicit windowed rate limits (such as the Rubin Science Platform's 1,000 requests per minute and 12 concurrent queries) are paced by a sliding-window rate limiter (`--limit-share`, default `0.85`).

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  R["A request"] --> C["Per-origin cap<br/>(--max-per-origin, default 4)"]
  C --> L["Windowed rate limiter, where the<br/>service publishes limits (--limit-share)"]
  L --> H["HTTP exchange"]
  H --> Q{"Transient failure?<br/>408 429 500 502 503 504,<br/>timeout, connection reset"}
  Q -- no --> D["Done"]
  Q -- yes --> E["Logged at ERR level and counted<br/>in the request ledger"]
  E --> B{"Retries left?<br/>(--retries, default 5)"}
  B -- yes --> W["Exponential backoff"] --> C
  B -- no --> F["Failed"]
```

Astro Data Lab's public TAP publishes no limits, so the `adl-healpix` adapter keeps to the conservative end of what was observed: at most 30 requests a minute and two at a time, at most 50 index ranges in a query (100 or more time out) and 50,000 rows back. It asks for nothing that needs a login, and no response header ever asked it to slow down. Details, and the cost of a match, are in [Data Lab without a login](datalab-healpix.md).

## 2. Dynamic mirror load balancing

Many HiPS surveys and the CDS `hips2fits` service are replicated across multiple international mirrors (CDS Strasbourg `alasky` and `alaskybis`, Harvard CfA, CADC, STScI, etc.).

- Before a HiPS cutout run begins, MOSAICS reads the survey's mirror list from the CDS MocServer registry and sends one lightweight validation probe to every candidate mirror.
- Surviving mirrors enter a live pool scored by `(in_flight + 1) * latency_ewma`. Each request is dispatched to the lowest-scored mirror.
- If a request fails on one mirror—even with a permanent HTTP error—the engine immediately re-attempts it on an untried mirror before backing off, temporarily benching mirrors that fail repeatedly.
- Pass `--no-mirrors` on `mosaics-cutout` to pin all requests to the primary host when debugging a specific server.

## 3. Single-node vs. multi-node execution (`mosaics-proxy`)

Because archive rate limits are enforced per source IP address, a single machine is bounded by one IP's quota. When other machines can lend their connection (cluster login nodes, cloud instances, workstations of collaborators), `mosaics-proxy` turns them into a distributed outbound request pool. A worker dials out to the pool and needs no open port; the pipeline only sees an ordinary HTTP proxy on the main node.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  P["MOSAICS pipeline<br/>(--proxy http://127.0.0.1:8888)"] --> S["mosaics-proxy server<br/>(main node)"]
  S -. "1. publishes the tunnel port" .-> G[("Announcement<br/>(encrypted, signed)")]
  W["Worker nodes 1 to N<br/>(dial out, no open port)"] -. "2. read it" .-> G
  W -- "3. SSH login and forward" --> H["SSH entry<br/>(login host)"]
  H -- "4. loopback tunnel; requests come back this way" --> S
  W --> A[("Archive")]
```

1. **Main node (`mosaics-proxy server`):** Runs locally, accepts HTTP proxy requests from any MOSAICS pipeline (`--proxy http://127.0.0.1:8888`), and schedules each request onto a remote node that has spare capacity for that target archive origin. With `--announce` it publishes where workers can reach it, so a worker started with only a name finds it.
2. **Remote nodes (`mosaics-proxy worker`):** Each reads the announcement, logs in to the SSH entry it names and opens a forward to the server's loopback tunnel port, so the connection runs worker → SSH entry → tunnel → server and the worker needs no inbound port. The server then monitors it through the `heartbeat@mosaics` SSH subsystem. The scheduler tracks each node's live goodput (bytes/s), connection latency, and error rate per archive origin, ordering available nodes by health without ever exceeding `--max-per-origin` on any single node.
3. **Graceful draining:** Sending `SIGTERM` to a worker or `POST /drain?worker=<id>` to the server's stats port drains in-flight requests cleanly without dropping active downloads. If a node disconnects before the first response byte arrives, the server transparently re-places the request on another node.
4. **Who carried what:** each worker has a name and reports a machine identity; the server keeps a ledger of sessions, and `mosaics-proxy workers` prints each name's contribution. A report from a multi-node run lists its nodes by name.

The commands, the announcement and the ledger are in the [`mosaics-proxy` reference](../cli/proxy.md). To lend a machine as a collaborator, see [Run a worker](../getting-started/run-a-worker.md).


# Crossmatching a table of positions

`mosaics-crossmatch run` takes **a table of positions** (a CSV, Parquet, FITS or VOTable file, any columns) and **one or more surveys**, and writes the table back with each survey's columns joined on. This page explains what a run does, how a survey says how it is to be matched, which adapter finds the pairs, and what to do when part of a run fails. The flags are in the [command reference](../cli/crossmatch.md) and the files it writes in the [output schema](../data-model/crossmatch.md).

## What a run does

1. **Reads the input** and finds its position columns (`--ra-col`, `--dec-col`, or inferred). A row without a finite position is never sent anywhere and comes back unmatched.
2. **Resolves each survey** from the roster (the survey files named by `--survey` or by `surveys:` in a job file, less `exclude:`): its catalogue, its `column_mapping`, its radius.
3. **Checks before it spends anything.** The columns every survey will add are settled, and two surveys (or a survey and the input) claiming one output name are refused; so is `--fov` on a survey that does not add the columns it needs. The only requests sent at this point list a table's columns.
4. **Matches the surveys one after another.** Each survey's matching is cut into **tasks**, each owning some of the input rows; a task is one upload, one cell, one set of index ranges. Finished tasks are cached beside the output.
5. **Reduces the pairs.** Every pair inside the radius is found; the nearest counterpart is kept per input row (`--all-matches` keeps every pair, for one survey).
6. **Joins the result onto the whole input** as a chain of left joins, so an input row never moves, and writes the table, the run account, the report and, if a task failed, the failures file.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  IN["Input table<br/>(any columns, with positions)"] --> A["1. Read the input,<br/>find the position columns"]
  A --> B["2. Resolve each survey:<br/>catalogue, column map, radius"]
  B --> C["3. Check before spending:<br/>output names, --fov columns"]
  C --> D["4. Match the surveys<br/>one after another"]
  D --> E["5. Reduce the pairs:<br/>nearest per input row, or all"]
  E --> F["6. Chain of left joins<br/>onto the whole input"]
  F --> OUT[("Output table, run account,<br/>report, failures file")]
```

Only `(key, ra, dec)` leaves your machine. The archive's columns are joined back onto the full input here.

## The survey's `crossmatch` section

A survey file describes how it is matched in its `crossmatch` section, next to the `column_mapping` that names the columns it brings:

```yaml
crossmatch:
  radius: 3 arcsec
  radius_note: PSF FWHM 6.1 to 12.0 arcsec in W1-W4; positions of high-S/N sources accurate to 50 mas.
  strategy: upload        # or: extract
  moc: allwise-moc.fits   # optional footprint, for --filter-moc
```

- **One radius per survey.** The radius is a property of the survey's depth and astrometry, so it lives with the survey and carries the note saying what it rests on. A match uses the survey's radius (the *library* value), unless a job's `overrides:` changes it or `--radius` names one for a single survey. The report says which of the three it used.
- **Prefixes.** The survey's columns come behind its prefix (`wise_mag_w1`), followed by `<prefix>_dist_arcsec`, the separation to the counterpart, and `<prefix>_nmatch`, how many counterparts lay inside the radius. `--prefix` changes a prefix for one survey and `--no-prefix` removes them (two surveys then may not share a column name).
- **Columns.** `column_mapping` maps remote column names to aliases and the loader adds the prefix. A key may be a pattern: `'[ugriz]pmag': mag_psf_{1}` selects the five columns and names each with the letter it matched. Patterns need the table's column list, so they work where an archive can be asked for it; `--columns` replaces the map for one survey with remote names or patterns.
- **Strategy.** `upload` sends the positions to the archive and gets the pairs back. `extract` is for a small catalogue, or for a selection that joins several tables and so cannot be an upload join: it fetches the survey's rows over each occupied HEALPix cell and the cells touching it, once, and matches here. An extract that reaches the service's row cap fails that cell and names the cap; it never falls back to uploading silently.

A spectroscopic survey is matched through its `target_selection` query, so its quality cuts apply and the columns are the query's aliases.

## Which adapter finds the pairs

The adapter is the `adapter` of the survey's catalogue entry. You change it with `overrides:` in a job file, or with an extension file that extends the library file and replaces the `catalog` list.

| Adapter | How the pairs are found | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| `tap`, `lsst` | The positions are uploaded to a TAP service and joined there. | the service; a token for Rubin (`LSST_TOKEN` or `--lsst-token`) |
| `adl`, `crossid` | The positions are uploaded to Astro Data Lab or SkyServer and joined there. | a login (`DATALAB_USER`, `DATALAB_PASSWORD`); Data Lab accounts can no longer be authenticated |
| `adl-healpix` | Rows in the sky pixels around the positions are fetched from Data Lab's public TAP by index range; the match is made here. | nothing; see [Data Lab without a login](datalab-healpix.md) |
| `lsdb` | A partitioned (HATS) catalogue is read partition by partition and matched with LSDB. | the catalogue's location |
| `local`, `nersc` | A catalogue downloaded once is matched on this machine with DuckDB. | disk for the file |

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  IN["Input positions"] --> AD{"The survey's<br/>adapter"}
  AD -- "tap, lsst, adl, crossid" --> U["Upload the positions;<br/>the archive joins them"]
  AD -- "adl-healpix" --> R["Fetch the rows of the sky pixels<br/>around the positions (index ranges)"]
  AD -- "lsdb" --> H["Read the HATS partitions<br/>that cover the positions"]
  AD -- "local, nersc" --> D["Range join with DuckDB<br/>on a downloaded file"]
  U --> P["Pairs inside the radius"]
  R --> M1["Match here<br/>(great-circle separation)"] --> P
  H --> M2["Match with LSDB"] --> P
  D --> P
  P --> N["Nearest counterpart per row<br/>(or every pair)"]
```

Credentials are never read from YAML.

## Footprints

`mosaics-crossmatch moc --survey X -o X-moc.fits` builds a survey's footprint as a Multi-Order Coverage map from its footprint table. `run --filter-moc` then leaves rows outside it out of the upload: they cannot match, and the archive is spared the bytes. The report counts them.

## When part of a run fails

An individual task is allowed to fail. After its retries (with a growing, jittered wait that honours `Retry-After`), the task is recorded, its rows are left empty for that survey, the survey is marked **incomplete** in the account and the report, and the other tasks and surveys go on. The failed tasks are listed in `<stem>.failures.parquet`.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  T["A task<br/>(one upload, cell or set of ranges)"] --> OK{"Succeeds?"}
  OK -- yes --> CA["Cached next to the output"]
  OK -- no --> RL{"Retries left?"}
  RL -- yes --> WT["Wait: growing and jittered,<br/>honouring Retry-After"] --> T
  RL -- no --> ST{"--strict?"}
  ST -- yes --> FL["The run fails;<br/>no table is written"]
  ST -- no --> RC["Recorded in the failures file;<br/>rows left empty; survey marked incomplete"]
  RC --> GO["Other tasks and surveys go on"]
```

Running the same command again repeats only what is missing, because finished tasks are cached next to the output, under `.mosaics-crossmatch/<output-stem>/`. `--overwrite-cache` ignores the cache. `--strict` turns a failed task into a failed run instead, and no table is written.

## Limits of the archives

Each archive's published or observed limits are enforced in the run, not left to retries: windowed rate limiters for Rubin and the public Data Lab TAP, a per-host cap on concurrent requests (`--workers`, `--limit-share`), and an upload sized from a real measurement rather than assumed (Rubin caps one upload near 33 MB). See [archive limits](archives.md). Every request, retry and wait is counted, and the report shows what each survey cost its archive.

## Extending a shipped survey for a crossmatch

The shipped survey files are a library you extend rather than edit. To match `wise` at 2 arcseconds against your own copy of a table, write a survey file that extends it:

```yaml
# my_wise.yaml
extends: surveys/wise.yaml
crossmatch:
  radius: 2 arcsec
catalog:
  - name: wise
    type: photometric
    adapter: tap
    adapter_params:
      service: https://example.org/tap
      table: my.allwise_copy
```

and name it: `mosaics-crossmatch run --survey my_wise -i targets.csv -o out.parquet`. The slug stays `wise`, so the columns keep their prefix. The same changes can be made for one run with `overrides:` in a job file, which is what the recipes show.

## Seeing the effective configuration

Every run logs the configuration it ended up with: the job files in play, each argument with where its value came from (default, flag or a file), and the survey definitions after the overrides, with what each override changed. The run account stores the same, so the report can say it.


# Cutout Backends & Routing

MOSAICS provides five interchangeable backends for image cutouts (`mosaics-cutout`), plus the `full` router that combines them across surveys and bands into a single Lance dataset. All backends write the exact same Arrow tensor schema and calibration metadata, so downstream training code never needs to know which backend produced a stamp.

## 1. The five backends

| Backend | How it works | Network cost | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `hips` (service) | Requests rendered FITS/JPEG/PNG stamps from the CDS `hips2fits` web service (load-balanced across `alasky` and `alaskybis`). | 1 HTTP request per target & band | Sparse target lists ($N \lesssim 10^4$) across any HiPS survey. |
| `hips --local` | Downloads HEALPix HiPS tiles from the survey's mirror pool into `~/.cache/mosaics/hips` and renders TAN-projected cutouts locally. | 1 download per unique sky tile (shared across neighbouring targets) | Dense or large target lists ($N \gtrsim 10^4$); verified to agree with `hips2fits` to float round-off. |
| `lsv` | Queries the Legacy Survey Viewer `fits-cutout` / `jpeg-cutout` HTTP API (`legacysurvey.org/viewer`). | 1 HTTP request per target (multi-band FITS stack returned in one call) | Medium runs on Legacy Survey (`ls-dr10`, `ls-dr11`), `ps1`, `hsc-dr3`, `sdss`, `galex`, `unwise-neo11`. |
| `nersc` | Downloads Legacy Survey $0.25^\circ \times 0.25^\circ$ brick coadds (`3600x3600` pixels) from the NERSC portal into `~/.cache/mosaics/bricks` and reprojects locally. | 1 brick download per band covering all targets in that $0.25^\circ \times 0.25^\circ$ brick | Large or clustered Legacy Survey DR11 runs where many targets share bricks. |
| `sia` / `vsa` | Queries an IVOA Simple Image Access (`sia`) or VISTA Science Archive (`vsa`) endpoint for science frames overlapping each target, caches the frames in `~/.cache/mosaics/fields`, and reprojects locally. | 1 metadata query + cached frame downloads | Surveys served only over SIA/VSA (`ukidss10`, `ukidss11`, `vhs5`, `viking`, `hst2`, `galex`). |

## 2. Spatial sorting for cache locality

When running a field-caching backend (`hips --local`, `nersc`, `sia`, `vsa`), nearby targets on the sky fall onto the same HiPS tiles, Legacy Survey bricks, or SIA science frames. Processing targets in random order would thrash the LRU disk cache (`--cache-size-gb`). MOSAICS therefore sorts targets spatially by HEALPix index before batching so that a cached tile or brick serves every target inside it before eviction.

## 3. How `mosaics-cutout full` routes bands

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  T["Target table"] --> D["Sky density and sample size"]
  D --> C["Cost model of each backend:<br/>latency, bandwidth, concurrency,<br/>render CPU time, download penalty"]
  C --> A["Each (survey, band) goes to the backend<br/>with the lowest estimated completion time"]
  A --> H["hips"]
  A --> V["lsv"]
  A --> N["nersc"]
  A --> S["sia / vsa"]
  H --> L[("One Lance dataset,<br/>one tensor schema")]
  V --> L
  N --> L
  S --> L
```

Several surveys declare more than one cutout backend in `defs/surveys/<slug>.yaml` (for example, `ls11` declares both `lsv` and `nersc`, and `ps1` declares both `lsv` and `hips`). When you run `mosaics-cutout full`:

1. It inspects the target list's sky density and sample size together with each backend's cost model (latency, bandwidth, concurrency, render CPU time, and per-GB download penalty).
2. It assigns each requested `(survey, band)` to the backend with the lowest estimated wall-clock completion time (or honours `--local` for HiPS surveys).
3. Pass `--plan` to print the chosen backend, pixel calibration unit, and estimated runtime for every `(survey, band)` without downloading any data:

```console
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.cutout full -t test/objects_sample_1k.csv -o cutouts.lance --config defs/cutout.yaml --plan
```

## 4. Pixel calibration metadata

Each cutout column (`cutout_<slug>_<band>`) records its physical calibration in the Arrow field metadata:

- `nanomaggy`: linear flux density where $m_{\text{AB}} = 22.5 - 2.5 \log_{10}(\text{flux})$ (`ls10`, `ls11`, `sdss20`, `unwise`).
- `ab_zeropoint` / `counts_per_s`: linear counts with a survey-wide AB zero point stored in `mosaics_scale` and `mosaics_offset` (`galex`, `hsc3`, `skymapper4`).
- `unknown`: uncalibrated display tiles (RGB `color` HiPS or per-frame zero points such as `vsa`/`sia`).


# Data Lab without a login: matching by index ranges

Astro Data Lab's large tables (`gaia_dr3.gaia_source`, `allwise.source`, `ukidss_dr11plus.lassource`, `ls_dr11.tractor`, ...) can be matched against a table of positions in two ways. The first uploads the positions to the archive and lets it join them, which needs a Data Lab account; accounts can no longer be authenticated, so that route is closed. The second, the **`adl-healpix`** adapter, needs neither a login nor an upload: it asks the archive's public TAP for the rows that lie in the sky pixels around the positions, and does the match on your machine. Since 2026-10-20 it is the route `wise`, `gaia3` and `ukidss11` ship with, and the way `ls11` is reached through Data Lab.

## The idea

Each of these tables carries a column, `nest4096`, holding the HEALPix NESTED index of the row's position at order 12 (4096 pixels along a base-pixel side, about 52 arcseconds across). The neighbours of a position are the rows whose index lies in a short list of ranges, so the archive is asked

```sql
SELECT <columns> FROM <table> WHERE nest4096 BETWEEN a AND b OR nest4096 BETWEEN c AND d OR ...
```

and nothing else: the anonymous service accepts neither an upload nor a spatial function, but it answers this. What comes back is a **superset** of the true matches, namely every row of every pixel the query covers. The match proper is made afterwards on your machine: every pair closer than the survey's radius, by great-circle (haversine) separation, is kept, and the nearest counterpart is chosen from those exactly as for any other adapter. The adapter's answer is therefore exact; the archive's only job is to return enough rows.

## How the positions are grouped

One request per position would be hopeless, so the planner groups the positions and writes the ranges for each group:

1. The sky pixels the positions' discs (the radius plus a hair) touch are found at order 12.
2. Positions are collected into blocks of sky, starting from large pixels (order 3). A block whose discs cover more than half of its pixel is asked for whole as one range; neighbouring ranges are merged when the rows expected in the gap between them are few.
3. A block becomes a query only if it respects three limits: at most **50 ranges** (the public TAP times out well above that), at most **50,000 rows** expected, and at most 100,000 positions; otherwise it is split into its four sub-blocks. Consecutive blocks are then packed into one query while they stay within the limits, so a sparse input makes few requests with many small ranges, and a dense one makes few requests with whole-pixel ranges.
4. The rows expected per query come from the table's density: the `rows_per_deg2` parameter when the survey file gives it, otherwise a count of the rows in the busiest (at most **eight**) sky cells of the input, kept so that a rerun asks nothing. The density only sizes the queries; the plan is exact whatever it is.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  P["Positions"] --> D["Order-12 pixels touched by<br/>each position's disc (radius plus a hair)"]
  D --> B["Collect into blocks of sky,<br/>starting at order 3"]
  B --> L{"Block within the limits?<br/>at most 50 ranges, 50,000 rows<br/>expected, 100,000 positions"}
  L -- no --> S["Split into its<br/>four sub-blocks"] --> L
  L -- yes --> PK["Pack consecutive blocks into one query<br/>while the limits hold"]
  PK --> Q["SELECT ... WHERE nest4096 BETWEEN a AND b OR ..."]
  Q --> M["Match here: every pair inside the radius<br/>by haversine separation"]
  M --> N["Nearest counterpart per input row"]
```

The plan is saved beside the results, so a rerun or a resume asks the same questions and repeats only what is missing.

## What can go wrong, and what the adapter does about it

- **A query returns its limit.** The answer is never trusted: the query is split into smaller ones and asked again. If one position's own neighbourhood holds more rows than the limit, the run says so and names the parameter to raise.
- **A query times out.** It is handled like a truncation, since asking again unchanged fails again.
- **The index is wrong.** On the first answer of each run the adapter recomputes the HEALPix pixel of the returned positions and compares it to `nest4096`. If any differ the survey is stopped with an error rather than risk missed matches. (This is why a table whose index column is mislabelled is safe to name: the run refuses it.)
- **The service is busy.** Requests are paced at **30 a minute, two at a time**. A crossmatch run matches its surveys one after another; in a targets run, where several steps can be in flight, every `adl-healpix` survey shares one allowance for the host. A 429 or 503 is retried with a growing, jittered wait that honours `Retry-After`; every failed attempt is logged as an error and counted in the request ledger.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  Q["A query is sent"] --> A{"The answer"}
  A -- "rows below the limit" --> K["Keep the rows"]
  A -- "reaches the limit, or times out" --> N{"More than one<br/>position in it?"}
  N -- yes --> S["Split the query and ask again"] --> Q
  N -- no --> E["Say so and name the<br/>parameter to raise"]
  A -- "429 or 503" --> R["Retry after a growing, jittered wait<br/>(Retry-After honoured)"] --> Q
  K --> F{"First answer of the run?"}
  F -- yes --> I{"Recomputed pixels equal<br/>nest4096?"}
  I -- no --> X["Stop this survey with an error"]
```

## Cost

Measured against the public TAP on 2026-10-20, matching within 5 arcseconds:

| Input | Table | Requests | Time | Rows returned | Pairs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000 positions in a 10 deg² field | `allwise.source` | 9 | 34 s | 64,857 | 67 |
| 10,000 positions in a 10 deg² field | `allwise.source` | 7 | 20 s | 147,992 | 813 |
| 1,000 positions spread over the sky | `allwise.source` | 22 plus 48 density counts | 28 s plus about 11 min of counts | 17,124 | 122 |
| 10,000 positions in a 10 deg² field | `gaia_dr3.gaia_source` | 4 | 11 s | 42,562 | 224 |

The price of a match is bytes, not requests: most rows returned are neighbours of a position in the same 52-arcsecond pixel, so between 0.1 % and 0.5 % of them become pairs. A sparse whole-sky input spends most of its requests on density counts, which is why they are capped at eight and why giving `rows_per_deg2` removes them. The report of a crossmatch shows, per survey, the queries sent, the ranges, the rows returned against the pairs found (the efficiency), the splits after a truncation and the limiter's state.

## Looking before sending

`mosaics-crossmatch run --dry-run` prints, for each `adl-healpix` survey, the plan it would send: the number of queries, ranges, positions per query, the rows expected and the minutes the requests would take at the pace above. It sends nothing; with no `rows_per_deg2` it assumes a typical density and says so.

## Using it

In a survey file the adapter is a catalog entry:

```yaml
catalog:
  - name: gaia3
    type: photometric
    adapter: adl-healpix
    adapter_params:
      table: gaia_dr3.gaia_source
      rows_per_deg2: 44000      # optional: skips the density counts
```

The table needs an index column (`index_column`, default `nest4096`, of order `index_order`, default 12), a pair of position columns (found by their UCD, or named with `remote_ra_column` and `remote_dec_column`) and nothing else; the keys are in the [configuration reference](../configuration/index.md).

To reach `ls11` this way, name the extension file instead of the library file; it swaps `ls11`'s catalog for `ls_dr11.tractor` and leaves everything else of the survey as it is:

```console
$ uv run -m mosaics.crossmatch.cli run --survey extensions/ls11-datalab -i targets.csv -o matched.parquet --fov ls11
```

It is for `mosaics-crossmatch` and `mosaics-fov`; the targets pipeline reads the Legacy Survey sweeps from NERSC for its own `ls11` extraction.

### In the targets pipeline

`mosaics-targets` runs the `adl-healpix` crossmatches the way it runs the others: one sky-cell store per survey (`augment/adl-healpix/<slug>`), filled cell by cell, a failed cell recorded and retried with `--retry-failed`. Nothing is uploaded and no login is needed. The cells of one survey are matched one after another, the queries of a cell side by side, and the survey shares the cap on steps per archive (`--steps-per-source`) with the other Data Lab steps. The store holds what the upload route's holds: the Legacy Survey identifier, the survey's columns under their prefix and the separation, so the catalogue is built from it unchanged.


# Field of view: the size of a galaxy's cutout

The **field of view** (`fov`) of a galaxy is the edge, in arcseconds, of the square cutout that frames it. It is the number that lets one dataset hold a faint compact galaxy and a bright extended one at a useful scale: the cutout of each is as wide as the galaxy needs, and the pixel scale varies with it. The targets catalogue carries it as the `fov` column, and `mosaics-cutout` reads it back to decide how much sky to request for each target.

Three commands compute it, with one set of numbers: `mosaics-targets` (the catalogue's `fov`), `mosaics-crossmatch run --fov SURVEY` (a column added after a match) and [`mosaics-fov`](../cli/fov.md) (any table).

## What it needs

The model is calibrated on the **Legacy Survey `r` band**, so its inputs are the Legacy Survey Tractor measurements of the galaxy:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `shape_r` | half-light radius of the galaxy model, arcseconds |
| `shape_e1`, `shape_e2` | the two ellipticity components of the galaxy model |
| `mag_r` | extinction-corrected `r` magnitude, or `flux_r` (model flux, nanomaggy) together with `mw_transmission_r` (Galactic transmission, linear, 0 to 1), from which it is made as $m_r = 22.5 - 2.5\log_{10}(\texttt{flux\_r} / \texttt{mw\_transmission\_r})$ |

A flux that is zero or negative, or a transmission that is not positive, has no magnitude. In the catalogue the columns are `ls11_shape_r` and so on; `mosaics-crossmatch` finds them under the survey's prefix (or bare when the run has no prefix), and `mosaics-fov` under `--prefix`.

## The three methods

Let $e = \min(\sqrt{e_1^2 + e_2^2},\; e_\mathrm{max})$ with $e_\mathrm{max} = 0.6$ (`--max-e`), so a near-degenerate fit cannot set the size. $c_\mathrm{ell}(m_r)$ and $c_\mathrm{circ}(m_r)$ are the correction factors of the ellipse and the circle, read from a table by $r$ magnitude that ships with MOSAICS (see [the correction factors](#the-correction-factors)).

| Method | What it measures | When it is used |
|---|---|---|
| **Ellipse** | the bounding box of the ellipse that $e_1$ and $e_2$ describe, with the ellipse's factor $c_\mathrm{ell}(m_r)$; $\mathrm{fov} = 2\,B\,c_\mathrm{ell}(m_r)$ converted to arcseconds, $B$ being the larger side of the bounding box of the ellipse of axes $1+e$ and $1-e$ at the position angle of the components ($B = 1$ when $e = 0$) | the default, wherever the ellipticity and the magnitude are known |
| **Circle** | twice the half-light radius with the circle's factor; $\mathrm{fov} = 2\,\texttt{shape\_r}\;c_\mathrm{circ}(m_r)$ | the default, only for a row with no usable ellipse |
| **Half-light ellipse** | the bounding box of the half-light ellipse of the galaxy model, scaled by the circle's factor (below) | only when asked for (`--hle`) |

Two things are worth knowing about the first two:

- **The ellipse form ignores `shape_r`.** Two galaxies with the same ellipticity and magnitude get the same size whatever their half-light radius.
- **The circle form ignores the ellipticity.** An edge-on disc and a round galaxy of one radius and magnitude get the same square.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  row([A row of the table]) --> mode{--hle given?}
  mode -- no --> ell{Ellipticity and<br/>magnitude known?}
  ell -- yes --> E[Ellipse form]
  ell -- no --> circ{Half-light radius<br/>and magnitude known<br/>and radius above 0?}
  circ -- yes --> C[Circle form]
  circ -- no --> none[No field of view<br/>counted under none]
  mode -- yes --> hle{Radius, ellipticity<br/>and magnitude known<br/>and radius above 0?}
  hle -- yes --> H[Half-light ellipse form]
  hle -- no --> none
```

### The half-light ellipse

The Legacy Survey Tractor catalogue describes a galaxy model by `shape_r`, `shape_e1` and `shape_e2`. In its documentation the ellipticity is the complex number $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_1 + i\,\varepsilon_2$: its modulus sets the axis ratio, $b/a = (1 - |\varepsilon|)/(1 + |\varepsilon|)$, and its phase the orientation of the major axis, $\varphi = \tfrac{1}{2}\arctan(\varepsilon_2/\varepsilon_1)$. `shape_r` is the half-light radius, and in the model it is the **semi-major axis** of that ellipse: the half-light ellipse has semi-axes $a = \texttt{shape\_r}$ and $b = \texttt{shape\_r}\,(1-e)/(1+e)$.

The half-light radius is not the radius that frames the galaxy. The circle's correction factor turns it into the one that does, $a' = c_\mathrm{circ}(m_r)\,\texttt{shape\_r}$, and this method frames the ellipse that has $a'$ as its semi-major axis and the same axis ratio and orientation:

$$
b' = a'\,\frac{1-e}{1+e}, \qquad
\mathrm{fov} = 2\,\max\!\Big(\sqrt{a'^2\cos^2\varphi + b'^2\sin^2\varphi},\; \sqrt{a'^2\sin^2\varphi + b'^2\cos^2\varphi}\Big)
$$

The square is the larger side of the ellipse's bounding box. A round galaxy ($e = 0$) gets exactly the circle's size, and an ellipse lying along an axis ($\varepsilon_2 = 0$) gets $2a'$: the edge is never longer than the corrected major axis. The ellipse's own factor $c_\mathrm{ell}$ plays no part: only the radius is corrected, so there is no second fit to make.

With `--hle`, **only** this method is used: a row with a half-light radius but no ellipticity (which the default would size with the circle) has no field of view. Choose the flag for a dataset in which the half-light radius should set the scale; leave it off to keep catalogues comparable with the ones built before it existed.

### Which method a row gets

By default each row takes the ellipse where it can and the circle where it cannot. A row is counted under the form it took, and under `none` when it took neither. The counts always list the four keys `ellipse`, `circle`, `half-light ellipse` and `none`; the forms the method does not use are zero.

### The correction factors

The factors that turn a size into the edge of the cutout come from a table by $r$ magnitude, one column for the ellipse and one for the circle, calibrated on Legacy Survey cutouts. Each column is read in one of two ways (`--interp`):

- `step` uses the value of the magnitude's own bin (the row of the integer magnitude);
- `linear`, the default, interpolates between the middles of the bins, so the value in the table is the factor at the magnitude plus one half.

Outside the table's range of 8 to 19 the factor of the nearest end is used, and a missing magnitude gives no field of view.

## Rows without a value

A row has **no field of view** when an input is missing or not finite, when no magnitude can be made from its flux, or when its size comes out as **zero**. A zero size arises from a half-light radius of zero with no ellipse to fall back on: no cutout of zero edge can be requested, so the value is empty rather than `0`.

A row with a missing input and a row of size zero are both empty, but the catalogue treats them differently, because the second one is a measurement (the object has no extent) and the first is the lack of one:

| Command | A row with a missing input | A row of size zero |
|---|---|---|
| `mosaics-fov` | is kept with an empty `fov`; `--drop-missing` leaves it out | the same |
| `mosaics-crossmatch run --fov` | is kept with an empty `fov` (so is every input row the survey did not match) | the same |
| `mosaics-targets` | is dropped from the catalogue, before the train/validation/test split is made | is **kept**, with an empty `fov` |

Both are counted under `none` in the report. `mosaics-cutout` fills every empty `fov` (and every value that is not above zero) with a default before it requests anything: the value of `--default-fov`, in the unit of `--fov-unit`, or, when it is not given, the **median of the valid `fov` values** of the table it reads. It logs how many targets got the default and which value. A table without any valid `fov` needs `--default-fov`.

## What each command writes

- The column is called `fov` (`--column` renames it in `mosaics-fov`), `float32`, in **arcseconds**, and a FITS or VOTable output carries its unit.
- Each command logs how many rows took each form. The crossmatch account records them with the method (`ellipse-or-circle` or `half-light-ellipse`), and the targets report shows them in the composition of the catalogue.
- `mosaics-crossmatch run --fov SURVEY` needs the survey to be one of those matched and to add the shape and magnitude columns; otherwise it is refused before any request. An input that already has a `fov` column is refused.

## Running it

```console
$ uv run -m mosaics.fov.cli -i matched.parquet -o with_fov.parquet --prefix ls11
$ uv run -m mosaics.fov.cli -i matched.parquet -o with_fov.parquet --prefix ls11 --hle
$ uv run -m mosaics.crossmatch.cli run --survey extensions/ls11-datalab -i targets.csv -o matched.parquet --fov ls11
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.targets --output out/ --hle
$ uv run -m mosaics.cli.cutout lsv -t targets.parquet -o lsv_grz.lance --layer ls-dr11 --bands grz --size 96 --fov-unit arcsec --default-fov 30
```

The second line sizes the table with the half-light ellipse alone; the third matches against `ls11` through Astro Data Lab's public TAP (see [Data Lab without a login](datalab-healpix.md)) and adds `fov` from the match; the fourth builds the catalogue with the half-light ellipse; the fifth cuts out a table in arcseconds and gives every target without a field of view 30 arcseconds.

```{warning}
`fov` is in **arcseconds**, and `mosaics-cutout` reads its field-of-view column in **arcminutes** unless told otherwise. Pass `--fov-unit arcsec` when cutting out targets from a table made by any of these commands, or every cutout will be sixty times too wide. `--default-fov` is in the same unit as the column (`--fov-unit`).
```

## Choosing the method for a catalogue

The default keeps every catalogue built so far valid. The half-light ellipse is a different size model: switching a catalogue to it changes the `fov` of every row, so the cutouts built from the old values no longer frame the same sky, and the choice belongs in the dataset's documentation. `mosaics-targets --hle` changes nothing that was fetched, only the size column and which rows survive (a row needs all of `shape_r`, `shape_e1`, `shape_e2` and the magnitude), so it is a cheap change to try.


# Variable-Length Spectra & Masking

Unlike image cutouts—which have a fixed `(C, H, W)` pixel shape chosen by the user—astronomical 1D spectra have **variable sample lengths** that depend on the spectrograph, arm coverage, and observation mode. That single fact shapes how `mosaics-spectrum` stores, masks, and resumes spectral datasets.

## 1. The four spectrum adapters

Each spectroscopic survey in `defs/surveys/` declares one or more `spectra:` entries using four backends:

| Adapter | How it fetches spectra | Surveys using it |
|---|---|---|
| `url` | Downloads each target's 1D spectrum FITS file from a URL column already present in the input table (`sixdfgs_access_url`, `hst_access_url`, `euclid_access_url`). | `6dfgs`, `hasp`, `euclidq1` |
| `template` | Builds the archive URL deterministically from target metadata columns (such as `plate`, `mjd`, `fiberid` for SDSS, `obsid` for LAMOST, or `serial` for 2dFGRS). | `sdss17`, `lamost11`, `2dfgrs` |
| `sparcl` | Queries the NOIRLab SPARCL service in batches by `targetid` (`dataset: DESI-DR1`). | `desi1` |
| `desi-healpix` | Downloads DESI `coadd-<survey>-<program>-<pix>.fits` HEALPix files from NERSC (`release: dr1`, `specprod: iron`), caches them locally, and splices the `B`, `R`, and `Z` spectrograph arms per target. | `desi1` |

## 2. Parallel arrays and atomic group semantics

For each spectroscopic survey `<slug>`, `mosaics-spectrum` writes up to four parallel Arrow `large_list` columns:

- `{slug}_flux` (`large_list<float32>`): 1D spectral flux density, scaled by `spectroscopic_system.flux_scale` when defined (standardised to $10^{-17}\ \text{erg}\ \text{s}^{-1}\ \text{cm}^{-2}\ \text{\AA}^{-1}$ for calibrated surveys).
- `{slug}_error` (`large_list<float32>`): $1\sigma$ uncertainty per spectral pixel in the **exact same unit as `{slug}_flux`**. Whether the archive publishes $1\sigma$ error (`ERROR`), variance (`VAR`), or inverse variance (`IVAR`), the decoder converts it to $1\sigma$ (`error = 1 / sqrt(ivar)` where `ivar > 0`, and `inf` where `ivar <= 0`). Surveys that publish no usable per-pixel uncertainty (`2dfgrs`, `6dfgs`) omit `{slug}_error`.
- `{slug}_wavelength` (`large_list<float32>`): wavelength per pixel in Angstroms ($\text{\AA}$).
- `{slug}_mask` (`large_list<bool>`): boolean usability mask where **`true` means usable (good pixel)** and **`false` means masked/unusable**.

Because these arrays describe the same 1D spectrum, they are guaranteed to have **identical length** on every row, and they succeed or fail as an atomic group.

## 3. Boolean `mask` and `--snr-floor`

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  P["A spectral pixel"] --> A{"flux and wavelength<br/>finite?"}
  A -- no --> M0["mask = false"]
  A -- yes --> B{"Archive bitmask<br/>zero (if any)?"}
  B -- no --> M0
  B -- yes --> C{"error finite and positive<br/>(if the column exists)?"}
  C -- no --> M0
  C -- yes --> D{"|flux| / error at least<br/>--snr-floor (if set)?"}
  D -- no --> M0
  D -- yes --> M1["mask = true"]
```

Archive bitmasks (`and_mask`, `ormask`, `DQ`, `B_MASK`) are consumed during decoding and never written raw to the dataset. Instead, each sample's boolean `mask[i]` is `true` if and only if all applicable conditions hold:

1. `flux[i]` and `wavelength[i]` are finite (`not NaN`, `not inf`).
2. The archive's own per-pixel quality bitmask is zero (when the archive provides one).
3. When `{slug}_error` exists, `error[i]` is finite and positive (`error[i] > 0`).
4. When `--snr-floor` is set (e.g. `--snr-floor 2.0`) and `{slug}_error` exists, $|{\text{flux}[i]}| / \text{error}[i] \ge \text{snr\_floor}$.

## 4. `null` vs. empty list (`[]`)

In a `large_list` column, an Arrow `null` and a zero-length list `[]` mean two distinct things:

- **Arrow `null`:** The download or decode **failed** (or the target was not observed by that survey). It is recorded in `.failures.parquet` and is eligible for `--retry-failed`.
- **Zero-length list `[]`:** The spectrum was fetched and decoded, but had zero samples. `--resume` treats a zero-length list as already completed and does not re-download it.


# Surveys, Entrypoints & the Prefix Rule

Every survey known to MOSAICS is described once, in a single YAML file under `defs/surveys/<slug>.yaml`. Whether you run `mosaics-cutout full`, `mosaics-spectrum`, `mosaics-targets`, or `mosaics-report db_constraints`, every pipeline reads the section it needs from that same file.

## 1. Separation of concerns inside a survey file

A survey file declares `survey_slug`, `name`, and whichever of ten independent sections apply to that survey:

| Section | What it describes | Read by |
|---|---|---|
| `catalog` | Remote or local catalogue tables (`photometric` or `spectroscopic`) and their provider adapter | `mosaics-targets`, `mosaics-query` |
| `catalog_filters` | Post-hoc DuckDB SQL depth/redshift quality cuts applied during catalogue production | `mosaics-targets` |
| `cutout` | Image cutout backends (`hips`, `lsv`, `nersc`, `sia`, `vsa`) and band lists | `mosaics-cutout full` |
| `spectra` | 1D spectrum download backends (`url`, `template`, `sparcl`, `desi-healpix`) | `mosaics-spectrum` |
| `photometric_system` | Passband SVO filter IDs, Vega/AB/asinh/linear conversion rules, and image pixel calibration | `mosaics-targets`, `mosaics-cutout` |
| `spectroscopic_system` | Fibre diameter, disperser, redshift tiebreak rank, velocity conversion, and flux calibration | `mosaics-targets`, `mosaics-spectrum` |
| `target_selection` | SQL query file (`.sql`) or HATS filter rules that seed the candidate table | `mosaics-targets`, `mosaics-report db_constraints` |
| `column_mapping` | Remote column to alias map for photometric crossmatching (glob keys select many columns); the loader adds the prefix | `mosaics-targets`, `mosaics-crossmatch` |
| `crossmatch` | The radius a table of positions is matched within, the note saying what it rests on, an optional footprint and the strategy | `mosaics-crossmatch`, `mosaics-targets` (the radius) |
| `provides` | Another survey's photometry already carried inside this survey's extraction query (e.g. `gaia3` and `unwise` inside `ls11`) | `mosaics-targets` |

Because each concern lives in its own section, editing a cutout backend cannot affect target selection, and changing a post-hoc `catalog_filters` cut only rebuilds the final production catalogue without refetching any sky cells.

## 2. Entrypoint files, `surveys:` and `overrides:`

The files in `defs/surveys/` are a **library**: one declarative, unfolded file per survey. A run reads them through an **entrypoint** (`defs/*.yaml`), the file `--config` takes, which lists the survey files it covers under `surveys:` (a string or list of paths/globs, `.yaml` optional), removes some with `exclude:`, and changes some under `overrides:`. `--config` also accepts a single survey file (`defs/surveys/ps1.yaml`), which is a run of that one survey.

```yaml
# defs/custom.yaml
surveys:
  - surveys/*

exclude:
  - surveys/lsst*

overrides:
  # Disable Pan-STARRS1 cutouts in this run:
  surveys/ps1:
    cutout: []
  # Remove the VHS DR5 post-hoc magnitude cut:
  surveys/vhs5:
    catalog_filters:
      vhs5: null
```

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  LIB["Library: defs/surveys/<br/>one file per survey"] --> RO
  EP["Entrypoint (--config):<br/>surveys, exclude"] --> RO["Roster"]
  CLI["--survey / --exclude-survey<br/>(replace / add)"] --> RO
  RO --> OV["overrides: merged over<br/>each surveys, least specific key first"]
  OV --> VA["Validated survey definitions"]
  VA --> LG["Logged as the effective configuration<br/>(library value -> effective value)"]
```

An override key is a glob over a survey file's name (`surveys/ps1`) or slug (`ps1`); every key that matches is merged deeply over the survey, the less specific key first. `--survey REF …` on the command line replaces the roster and `--exclude-survey REF …` adds to `exclude:`. Every run logs the effective configuration, naming each key an override changed as `library value -> effective value`.

`extends:` is a plain dictionary default and nothing else: an entrypoint extends entrypoints, and a survey file extends survey files. To change a library survey permanently for your own runs, write a survey file that extends it and list that file in place of the library one:

```yaml
# my_ps1.yaml
extends: surveys/ps1.yaml
cutout: []
```

Resolution rules:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  N["A relative path or glob<br/>(extends, surveys, exclude)"] --> A{"In the directory of<br/>the naming file?"}
  A -- yes --> W["Use it<br/>(warn if it also exists further on)"]
  A -- no --> B{"In $CWD?"}
  B -- yes --> W
  B -- no --> C{"In the package defs/?"}
  C -- yes --> W
  C -- no --> X["Error<br/>(an exclude: entry may match nothing)"]
```

- **Search order:** Relative paths in `extends:`, `surveys:` and `exclude:` are resolved first against the directory of the naming file, then `$CWD`, then the package `defs/` directory (deduplicated by resolved path). The first base where the path or glob matches wins; if found under multiple distinct bases, a warning is logged naming the winner and shadowed paths.
- **Recursive:** Files can extend files of their own kind to any depth. Circular extensions are detected and raise an error showing the full chain.
- **Exclusion:** An `exclude:` key removes matching files from the roster; an `exclude:` entry that matches nothing is allowed and logged at `info`.
- **Root lookup:** When passing `--config <file>`, relative paths are checked as given (in `$CWD`) and then in `defs/`, so `--config targets.yaml` works from any working directory; the repository-root spelling `--config defs/targets.yaml` resolves from anywhere too.

Shipped entrypoints in `defs/`:

- `defs/full.yaml`: globs all 30 files in `defs/surveys/*.yaml`.
- `defs/targets.yaml`: the production target-selection and crossmatch configuration.
- `defs/cutout.yaml`: all surveys with enabled cutout backends.
- `defs/lsv.yaml`: Legacy Survey Viewer cutout subset.

## 3. The prefix rule

Every column contributed by a survey catalogue carries that catalogue's prefix so columns from different archives never collide:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  R["Remote column<br/>ra"] --> M["column_mapping alias<br/>ra"] --> P["Prefix of the catalogue<br/>added by the loader"] --> O["Output column<br/>wise_ra"]
```

- A survey with a single catalogue uses `{slug}` as its prefix (e.g. `ls11_ra`, `vhs5_mag_aper3_ks`, `sdss17_z`).
- A survey declaring **both** a photometric and a spectroscopic catalogue in the same file appends `p` and `s` (`euclidq1p_*` and `euclidq1s_*`) so both halves have distinct coordinate and ID columns.
